note: Cost of living demand across the nine cohort markets. The source covers 199 countries and only about 200 country and market pairs had ever been measured, so the binding constraint on this family was never the data, it was the measurement. This probe exists to lift that constraint.
caution: A discovery probe, not a census. Each market was asked for its head term in phrase match and the top rows by volume were kept, so a country below the row limit is absent from this file and that absence is not evidence that nobody searches for it. The head terms are not translations of one another and volumes are comparable across markets only as orders of magnitude. A difficulty of zero means the provider judged it easy; a null means the provider had no estimate, which for a ten a month keyword is itself the finding. The Japanese block was constructed rather than discovered and says so in its own method field.

nl-NL.head: levensonderhoud
nl-NL.finding: Shallow and mostly not about countries at all: the head term is dominated by domestic benefit and child maintenance queries (nibud, pleegkind, aftrek). Country terms exist but run 10 to 30 a month. This tempers the earlier SERP finding that Dutch is the easiest market to enter: it is easy because there is very little there.

de-DE.head: lebenshaltungskosten

rows.keyword: wie hoch sind die lebenshaltungskosten in deutschland

de-DE.finding: Both word orders are live again, as in the best time probe, and again they are not the same keyword: `lebenshaltungskosten portugal` is 350 and `portugal lebenshaltungskosten` is 250. Difficulty is zero on almost every country term, which makes German the deepest genuinely winnable market for this family.

pl-PL.head: koszty życia
pl-PL.finding: Polish inflects the country and the locative is the only form that appears, which is why the resolver needed an alias table before it could read this market at all. Both word orders are live. Demand is broad rather than deep: fifty countries between 30 and 150 a month.
